title: MA9-05613
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: This is a de novo case. On December 11, 2012, the Federal Court allowed the judicial review of a Refugee Protection Division decision dated April 27, 2012, and referred the matter to be analyzed by a differently constituted panel.

The principal claimant is XXXX XXXX XXXX, born on XXXX XXXX XXXX 1964, in Mexico. He is accompanied by his wife, XXXX XXXX XXXX, born on XXXX XXXX XXXX 1971, in Mexico, and their son, XXXX XXXX XXXX, born on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2002, in Mexico. The claimants are all citizens of Mexico and are claiming refugee protection under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The principal claimant (hereafter the male claimant) was appointed as the designated representative for his minor son.
The male claimant's allegations are as follows, summarized from question 31 of his Personal Information Form (PIF):
He lived with his family in XXXX, XXXX XXXX.

On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, at about 9:00 p.m., he and his wife were driving toward their home, which is located about 20 minutes away from XXXX. Before arriving home, the male claimant was forced to stop because a vehicle with tinted windows blocked their path. Two masked men with high-calibre guns exited the vehicle.

They violently forced the claimants out of their vehicle, while uttering threats and insults, and forced them into their car. The men searched their car, threatening to kill them. The male claimant asked them who they were and what they were looking for, but they responded with a series of threats and insults. His wife experienced a serious nervous shock, and she began to cry and scream.

The men took the claimants' identity documents, and eventually one of the men told the other that they had the wrong people. To this, the other replied that, in any case, they had to kill the claimants to keep them quiet. The male claimant swore to keep quiet, and the men released them but warned them not to speak of the incident.

On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, the male claimant had to have his wife seen by a psychotherapist for her to recover from the trauma that she experienced. His wife nonetheless has nightmares, she can no longer sleep at night, and she is always very emotionally fragile.

On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, the male claimant went to the public ministry and the XXXX municipal police to file a complaint, but they did not believe him. He then returned to these locations numerous times to request an investigation, but he was continually told to return the next day.

His statement was finally taken at the XXXX public ministry on XXXX XXXX, 2009. The male claimant subsequently made several calls to learn more about his file, but he was always told that there was nothing new or that he should call back the next day.

Following his complaint, he noticed that there were suspicious people watching the house and lurking nearby. On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, a neighbour called the male claimant at work to tell him that there were armed people looking for him. The neighbour responded that he did not know the male claimant.
After his neighbour's call, the male claimant was unable to return home due to fear. On the same day, the family went to stay with relatives.
On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, the male claimant left Mexico for Canada. He claimed refugee protection on March 25, 2009.
The female claimant's allegations are as follows, summarized from her PIF:

On XXXX XXXX, 2009, when her husband left the country, he left the female claimant and their son at the home of relatives in a village near their city. On XXXX XXXX, 2009, the female claimant returned to her home in XXXX. All seemed quiet, but she was worried and distraught. She continued her therapy.

On XXXX XXXX, 2009, she received a telephone call from someone claiming to be a police officer and who asked to speak with her husband. The person asked her whether she was his wife, but because she was afraid, the female claimant stated that she was a neighbour. The person did not leave a message, but told the female claimant that they would call back later.
From that day on, the female claimant stopped answering the telephone and withdrew her son from school. On the night of XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, she barely slept and had nightmares.

The following day, the female claimant told her therapist-who had been wondering whether there was something in her past that could explain her level of anxiety-that her child had died in a motor vehicle accident in 1995 and that she herself had been hospitalized for 15 days. The claimants sued the insurer, but the owner of the bus took it personally and threatened them. They decided to drop the charges. In XXXX 2002, they had another child, and they decided to go live in XXXX XXXX.

On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, a suspicious vehicle parked on the corner of the street, a few metres away from the female claimant's house. One person got out and stayed there for about one hour, looking toward the house, as though looking or waiting for someone.
Thereafter, the female claimant stopped going out to the street and started to miss work. She was very afraid, and she asked her relatives to help her travel to Canada to join her husband.
On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, she left Mexico, arrived in Canada on the same day, and claimed refugee protection on the following day.

Should they return to Mexico, the claimants fear being killed by the people who stopped them on XXXX XXXX, 2009, and targeted them following the male claimant's complaint. The male claimant alleges that they are members of organized crime, that is, members of Los Zetas or the XXXX Cartel.
The male claimant also alleged a fear of extortion should he return to Mexico because, returning from Canada, he would be perceived as wealthy.

In light of the claimants' allegations, the panel determines that their claims for refugee protection have no nexus to one of the Convention grounds. The panel will therefore analyze them under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA.
The panel determines that the claimants are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection" for the following reasons. ANALYSIS Identity
The claimants' identities, including their citizenship, were established by means of the filed supporting documentation, namely, a copy of their passports. Credibility

In support of their claims for refugee protection, the claimants submitted the female claimant's psychosocial follow-up file at the Centre de santé et de services sociaux (CSSS) [Health and Social Services Centre] in Montréal. Follow-ups were conducted from XXXX 2011 to XXXX 2012 by a clinical nurse and a social worker. Their reports mention what the female claimant told them during their conversations. The female claimant told them that she had lost her two-and-a-half-month-old son in a motor vehicle accident about 15 years ago and that she herself had multiple fractures and underwent several operations. She stated to the case workers were that following the insurance claim made to the transport company by her husband, the bus driver who struck the female claimant's car made death threats. As a result, she and her husband left the city they were living in, fearing the death threats, and withdrew the charges. She told the CSSS case workers that she experienced a great deal of stress in the city where they settled because the political climate had become terrifying. She spoke of the XXXX 2009 attack committed by guerillas, drug traffickers, or criminals (the term varies throughout the reports) and the fact that she and her husband were threatened with death if they revealed anything. She stated that she and her husband moved to Quebec for that reason. She told the case workers that her major problem is that she has nightmares of losing the child she has now. She added that even if she lives peacefully here, she has recurring nightmares that terrify her. She stated that the trigger was the XXXX 2009 attack in Mexico and that she wants to get help for her recurring nightmares. She is afraid of sleeping and she lives with an accumulation of fatigue and sadness.

The female claimant did not speak to her psychosocial follow-up case workers about the complaint that her husband allegedly filed with the Mexican authorities following the XXXX 2009 attack. She did not speak to them about the fact that, according to the allegations in support of the refugee protection claim, following the complaint, some suspicious and armed people were looking for her husband, such that the family had to go live at an aunt's home and her husband had to leave the country shortly thereafter, that is, on XXXX XXXX, 2009. The female claimant also did not mention to the CSSS case workers the suspicious call that she allegedly received on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, asking for her husband, and did not tell them that she saw a suspicious person near her home on XXXX XXXX, 2009. However, according to her allegations, these two incidents resulted in her no longer answering the telephone, withdrawing her son from school, remaining indoors, and missing work. Still according to her allegations, it was following these incidents that she asked her relatives to help her travel to Canada with her son in order to join her husband.

When asked about the significant omissions in the statements she made to the CSSS case workers, the claimant stated that she did not remember whether she spoke to them about these incidents because she spoke to them about many things. The panel is not satisfied with these explanations. The claimants' refugee protection claim is based on their allegations that they were targeted after the male claimant did not follow the orders of the individuals who stopped them on XXXX XXXX, 2009, by filing a complaint against them. On reading the psychosocial reports submitted, the panel notes that the female claimant did not speak to the CSSS case workers about these significant incidents, namely, her husband's complaint, the threats and the subsequent suspicious incidents. The panel therefore draws a negative inference with respect to the credibility of the claimants' allegations that the male claimant had nonetheless decided to file a complaint with the authorities regarding the incident of XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, resulting in them subsequently being targeted.

At the hearing, the male claimant testified on several occasions before the panel that March 17, 2009, was the first time that he filed a complaint with the authorities in his country and that he had never had problems with anyone before. He testified that he filed a complaint with the XXXX public ministry, at the office of the attorney general for the state. He testified that since he filed a complaint with the police, members of the police had allegedly reported him to the individuals who stopped him on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009. He told the panel that he did not file a complaint against the police officers who allegedly reported him because filing a complaint against the authorities is complicated and because he does not know who is more dangerous between the police and the criminals. However, later in the hearing, during his lawyer's question period, the male claimant stated that it was not the first time that he had had problems, that he had experienced other acts of violence in the past and that he had always had bad experiences with the authorities. He then explained to the panel that following a motor vehicle accident in 1995, his child, who was on a bus with his wife, died. His wife sustained fractures all over her body. He testified at the hearing that when he filed a complaint with the public ministry to obtain compensation for all the damages sustained, he received death threats from the owner of the bus. He testified that the owner of the bus corrupted the authorities, who therefore took his side. Instead of compensation, he received threats. He testified that he withdrew his complaint and that he and his wife had their second son and moved to XXXX in 2002.

Whereas the male claimant initially testified that he had never had problems with anyone in the past and had never filed a complaint before the one to the public ministry on XXXX XXXX, 2009, he later testified that he had filed a complaint with the public ministry around 1995, had received death threats and had therefore withdrawn his complaint. After the hearing, the male claimants' lawyer filed additional submissions dated July 8, 2013, in which she mentions that the claimants want to clarify that they never filed a complaint in this matter, but merely followed up on a procedure that was established ex officio by the authorities. They produced Exhibit D-4(11), that is, an Internet document from the Federal District on road crimes. The document states that there are two types of these crimes: those that require a complaint in order for the authorities to acknowledge them and those that are prosecuted ex officio. It states that crimes that are prosecuted ex officio are those which, even without any complaint, the authorities are forced to acknowledge and investigate, including homicide and the abandonment of victims.

The panel notes that, according to this document, the possibility of filing a complaint, even for road crimes that must be prosecuted ex officio, is not excluded. The male claimant's initial testimony at the hearing was clearly to the effect that he had filed a complaint with the public ministry following the 1995 accident but that he subsequently withdrew his complaint. Therefore, the panel is of the opinion that the male claimant attempted to adjust his testimony to explain his contradiction regarding the number of complaints he has allegedly made in his lifetime. His credibility is undermined with respect to the complaint he claims he filed against those who stopped him on XXXX 2009, which he had initially identified as the first complaint he had ever made in his life (before contradicting himself by testifying that he previously filed a complaint in 1995).

The claimant testified that he went to the public ministry and to the XXXX municipal police for the first time on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, in an attempt to file a complaint. He added that it was the Monday following the incident of XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009. However, based on his narrative, he went to the public ministry and the municipal police for the first time on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009. This is an additional inconsistency in the male claimant's evidence, which undermines his credibility with regard to his alleged complaint.

The male claimant testified that on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, while he and his wife were on the road in their car, they were stopped by two masked and armed individuals. These individuals violently forced the claimants to exit of their vehicle in order to enter their vehicle. They searched their vehicle as they threatened and insulted the claimants, but released them after they realized that they had the wrong people. However, as a condition of their release, the claimants were not to speak of the incident to anyone. The male claimant testified that he was detained for half an hour, an hour. He testified that he attempted, on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, to file a complaint with the XXXX public ministry and with the city's municipal police but that they did not believe him. He alleged that he repeatedly returned to these two locations to file a complaint but that they did not record the information he gave and he was told to return the next day. Finally, on XXXX XXXX, 2009, he managed to file a complaint with the XXXX public ministry. In this regard, he filed a copy of the complaint as Exhibit D-4(4). He stated that the authorities gave him the copy of the complaint without him asking for it.

The panel notes that the document simply mentions that the offence in question is [translation] "attempted deprivation of personal liberty," without further details, for instance, about the number of individuals in question, what they looked like or how they were dressed, whether they were armed, the timeline of the incident, or the threats received. Neither the date and time nor the location of the incident is mentioned.

When asked by the panel why the complaint submitted states that it was attempted deprivation of liberty when the male claimant's allegation is that he was in fact forcibly confined for a half an hour or more, he stated that he had explained to the officer who received his complaint what had happened and that that is what she wrote. When asked whether he had provided the details to the officer, he responded that he had. When asked whether he had the opportunity to reread his testimony and make corrections to it, he replied that he did not.

However, the objective documentary evidence1 states that when filing a complaint with the public ministry or the office of the attorney general, at both the federal and state level, the complainant must describe what happened as precisely as possible when making his statement, read it over, and can make corrections to his testimony. When confronted with this inconsistency, the male claimant responded that, in fact, what is described in the objective documentary evidence is the entire procedure. He added that it was what he intended to do but that, following his complaint, people were pursuing him and he did not have time to return to the public ministry to add to his statements or follow up on the investigation. The male claimant's statements do not explain why the complaint in question indicates that it was an attempt to deprive liberty when, according to his allegations, it was not an attempt.

Additionally, whereas the male claimant stated at the hearing that he did not have the opportunity to make corrections to his statement at the time of the complaint, that he did not see the officer's notes and that he was not given anything to sign; the objective documentary evidence indicates the contrary. The panel prefers to attach more weight to the objective documentary evidence than to the male claimant's testimony.

Furthermore, the panel notes the lack of substantive information on the complaint filed by the male claimant (namely, the date, time and location of the incident, the number of individuals in question, what they looked like or how they were dressed, whether they were armed, the timeline of the alleged incident, the threats received). It should be reiterated that, according to the objective documentary evidence, a detailed statement is recorded on the complaints.

The panel also considered the three invoices from psychological consultations that the female claimant attended in Mexico, submitted in Exhibit D-4(1). They are dated XXXX XXXX, 2009, XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, and XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009. However, these invoices do not indicate the reasons for the female claimant's consultations and therefore have little probative value in establishing the alleged threats following the incident of XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009.

The claimants also filed under D-4(2) a letter from a physician and surgeon which mentions that on XXXX XXXX, 2009, the female claimant went to the medical unit with acute anxiety disorder and a panic attack. The physician added that she was referred to the psychiatric unit in the city of XXXX. However, this document does not establish that the claimants were threatened after the attack of XXXX XXXX, 2009.

In light of the elements mentioned above, the panel finds that the claimants did not credibly establish that they filed a complaint against the individuals who stopped them on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, or that they were targeted in 2009 because of this complaint, as alleged. Although the benefit of the doubt could have been given with regard to some of these elements when considered in isolation, these elements considered together lead the panel not to believe the filed complaint and, consequently, the ensuing threats.

In any case, even if the claimants had been able to establish that they had filed a complaint in 2009 and were targeted in 2009 following this complaint, the panel is of the opinion that the prospective risk, on a balance of probabilities, would not exist if they were to return to Mexico today. Prospective risk

It should be noted that in the prospective risk analysis, the panel will also analyze the credibility of the allegations of threats that the claimants apparently received after 2009, while they were in Canada.

At the hearing, when asked by the panel about his fears should he return to Mexico after spending over four years in Canada, the male claimant stated that his neighbours informed him that the individuals who stopped him during the incident on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, are still looking for him and that they threatened his neighbours. He stated that he fears being found anywhere he goes in Mexico by reason of the power of the people in the organized group that allegedly targeted him, and he added that they considered the complaint that he filed as a personal affront.

At the hearing, the male claimant also stated that he is unable to move elsewhere in Mexico because he is afraid that criminal groups operate under different names in different regions and that they are interconnected.

However, the panel does not believe, on a balance of probabilities, that the male claimant and his family would be troubled by the individuals who allegedly stopped them during the incident on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, if they were to return to Mexico, for the following reasons.
First, the claimants were unable to identify their two attackers during the incident of XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009, as they were masked and unwilling to be identified.

As such, the male claimant is only speculating that his attackers were members of either the Los Zetas group or the XXXX Cartel. In fact, he testified at the hearing that in the region of XXXX XXXX, where he lived and was stopped, the members of organized crime are those who commit assaults, but he could not confirm what organized group he had dealt with. When the panel reminded him that, based on his update to question 31 of his PIF,2 he believed that his attackers were members of Los Zetas (and noted that this group was associated with the XXXX Cartel), the male claimant stated that Los Zetas and the XXXX Cartel operate in his area and that they commit crimes against the population. The panel therefore notes that the male claimant, who was not at all able to identify the two individuals who stopped him on XXXX XXXX, 2009, is only making assumptions with respect to their identity. The male claimant was thus unable to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that the people who would target him, according to his allegations, are indeed members of Los Zetas and the XXXX Cartel.

Moreover, the male claimant's allegations are to the effect that, at the time of the incident, the individuals were looking for people other than the male claimant and his wife, who were themselves then released. Therefore, the male claimant and his wife were not targets or persons of significance for these individuals. In addition, there was no follow-up to the alleged complaint: the individuals were not stopped by the Mexican authorities. Consequently, it is not credible that, after several years, the claimants would interest the individuals in question such that they would be motivated enough to make efforts and deploy resources to search for the claimants.

It should also be noted that to demonstrate that he is still wanted by his alleged agents of harm, the male claimant produced letters from neighbours and friends3 indicating that suspicious people are lingering around the male claimant's house and asking questions about the male claimant's contact information and that they are threatened by individuals who demand to know the male claimant's whereabouts. These letters refer to an incident in XXXX 2011 and incidents in XXXX 2012 and in 2013.

However, the male claimant, who alleged that these letters were sent to him by DHL, was unable to submit envelopes used for the mailing because he did not keep them. It should be noted that none of these letters are handwritten.

The letter from a neighbour, XXXX XXXX,4 was then produced by the male claimant to establish his allegations at his first hearing on March 1, 2012, (before a different panel) that he was aware that he was still being sought by communicating with neighbours in XXXX 2011.5 This letter was not submitted at his first hearing before the other panel. The male claimant also produced, at his second hearing before this panel on June 27, 2013, letters directly addressed to him that refer to incidents in XXXX 2012 and in 2013 in which individuals were seeking his whereabouts. The panel notes that the male claimant did not produce any letters referring to the fact that he was being sought between XXXX 2011 and XXXX 2012, that is, for a one-year period. Aside from the letter produced to support his allegations at his first hearing (search for the male claimant in XXXX 2011), the male claimant now produced only letters that refer to incidents that took place only a few months before his second hearing on June 27, 2013. However, these letters from friends are addressed to him personally. If it were true that individuals are still looking for the male claimant since his departure from Mexico in XXXX 2009, he should have received more letters from friends indicating that he was being sought between XXXX 2011 and XXXX 2012; in other words, there should have been continuity in these searches.

For all the aforementioned reasons, the panel is of the opinion that the letters in question produced by the male claimant have no probative value. His credibility with regard to the current threats is undermined.

The male claimant alleges that the individuals searching for him are either members of Los Zetas or members of the XXXX Cartel, a group associated with Los Zetas, according to him. He testified before the panel that he fears that these groups will find him anywhere he goes in Mexico because of their economic influence and manpower. He added that the different criminal groups are interconnected or operate under different names in various regions of the country. However, if that were the case, the individuals allegedly looking for him, who are members of a powerful criminal organization according to the male claimant, ought to have known that he left the country several years ago. In fact, the objective documentary evidence indicates that Los Zetas is reportedly the most technologically advanced, sophisticated and dangerous cartel in Mexico.6 Instead, the male claimant produced letters (mentioned above) to the effect that individuals are allegedly still looking for him, including in the neighbourhood where he lived when he was in Mexico. Therefore, the male claimant's various allegations are internally inconsistent, and his credibility with regard to the current threats is undermined.

The male claimant filed a letter from his wife's aunt, as well as a letter from his wife's cousin,7 which are both dated March 15, 2013. These letters state that the cousin was kidnapped in the state of XXXX for ransom and that the kidnappers told the aunt (the cousin's mother), who had no money, to ask her niece in Canada-the female claimant-to give them money. At the hearing, the male claimant also testified that the kidnappers told the mother of the cousin who had been kidnapped to ask her family in Canada-the claimants-to give her money.

The male claimant testified at the hearing that he could not live peacefully elsewhere in Mexico because all the criminal groups are interconnected and because they would be able to find him anywhere. If that were the case, the kidnappers of the cousin in XXXX, who became aware as early as March 2013 or even before that the claimants are in Canada, could have given this information to Los Zetas or to the XXXX Cartel, the male claimant's alleged agents of harm. However, the male claimant produced letters from friends and neighbours dated after XXXX 2013 which state that his agents of harm are still looking for him in Mexico. When asked to explain this inconsistency, the male claimant answered that he did not know why the cousin's kidnappers found out that he was in Canada and that his neighbours stated that he is still being sought. The panel is not satisfied with the male claimant's explanations and is of the opinion that it is an additional inconsistency in the male claimant's evidence, which undermines his credibility regarding the current threats.

During her submissions, counsel for the male claimant stated that the kidnappers of the cousin in XXXX did not identify themselves and that, consequently, it is not known whether they have ties to the alleged agents of harm and that it could be local crime. However, even if this were the case, it would be inconsistent for petty local criminals in XXXX to be aware that the claimants are in Canada when powerful organizations such as Los Zetas and the XXXX Cartel are not aware and are still looking for him in Mexico, as alleged by the male claimant. Once again, his credibility with regard to the current threats is undermined.

In light of all the elements noted above, even if the panel believed (which is not the case) that the claimants filed a complaint in 2009 against individuals who stopped and then targeted them in 2009, it is of the opinion that, on a balance of probabilities, the male claimant and his family would not be targeted if they were to return to Mexico today. Analysis of the fear of extortion alleged by the male claimant

In the update to question 31 of his PIF,8 the male claimant stated that, should they return to Mexico, he and his family would face a risk of being extorted because people would think that they are wealthy given that they lived in Canada.

However, at the hearing, when the panel asked the male claimant if he had fears other than his fear of the group that is supposedly involved in organized crime, by reason of his report to the authorities, the male claimant answered that he did not. The panel then reminded the male claimant of the alleged fear of extortion in the update to his PIF, to which he responded that it was his wife's cousin who was forcibly confined and that the problems were not directly related to him. He then made reference to the letters from his wife's aunt and her cousin, previously mentioned by the panel.9

It was only when the panel asked the male claimant whether he would fear extortion if he returned to Mexico that he hesitated, before answering yes. He then claimed that because he and his family had lived in Canada, the criminal groups would think that they have money and would extort them.

The panel must note that, during his hearing, the male claimant did not mention the fear of extortion from the outset. It was only after the panel reminded him of what he had stated in his PIF, and after hesitating, that he claimed to be afraid of extortion if he had to return to his country.

Furthermore, although the male claimant stated that he could be extorted because he would be perceived to be a wealthy person returning to Mexico from Canada, the panel notes that the objective documentary evidence is silent on this topic. Similarly, the male claimant provided no evidence to support his allegation, apart from the letter from his wife's cousin, who lives in the state of XXXX, which was previously mentioned by the panel.10 In that letter, the cousin wrote to the female claimant that his kidnappers, knowing that the female claimant was in Canada, demanded that his mother (the cousin's mother) ask the female claimant for money. The cousin also wrote that if the female claimant returned to Mexico, the kidnappers would think that she is bringing a large sum of money and that she and her family would be at risk there.

The male claimant himself stated at the hearing that the kidnapping of the cousin was not a problem directly related to him. In addition, based on the letters from the cousin and the cousin's mother, he is no longer being detained by his kidnappers, at least since March 15, 2013, the date on which the cousin allegedly wrote the letter to the female claimant. Consequently, the cousin's letter has little probative value in establishing that the claimants would be targeted and extorted should they return to their country.

Considering all the above, the panel is of the opinion that the male claimant did not discharge his burden of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that he would be targeted by criminals if he returned to his country because he would be perceived as wealthy. The evidence on the record does not establish the existence of a prospective risk on a balance of probabilities.

Moreover, even if the claimants would indeed be targeted by reason of their perceived wealth should they return to their country, this would be a generalized risk: the claimants would not face a personal risk that is not faced generally by other individuals in Mexico. The risk of being targeted by crime is generalized and borne by all Mexicans.

In fact, the objective documentary evidence11 indicates that Mexicans from all social classes, including those in the middle and lower classes, can be kidnapped for ransom. Further, since Calderón's presidency, the rates of reported crimes such as homicide, kidnapping, extortion and violent robbery have significantly increased, and a growing number of victims unrelated to drug cartels have been targeted by gangs.12 Female claimant's health condition

At the hearing, the claimants also alleged that if they had to return to Mexico, they would fear for the female claimant's frailty. The male claimant alleged that if they had to settle elsewhere in Mexico, his wife would live with a constant fear of their son being kidnapped and that she has recurring nightmares. Their lawyer submitted that the female claimant testified that she lived in constant fear in Mexico and that the mere fact of being in Mexico would aggravate her fragile emotional state. The lawyer submitted that it would be unreasonable for her to go to Mexico.

As previously mentioned, the claimants filed the female claimant's CSSS psychosocial follow-up reports, dated 2011 and early 2012.13 The claimant told the case workers about the problems surrounding the death of her son in 1995 and the attack of XXXX XXXX, 2009. She told them that she has nightmares and explained her various troubles. The case workers alleged that the female claimant has depressive symptoms: depression, sadness, crying, low energy, difficulty sleeping. The diagnosis is that there are post-traumatic elements and symptoms of anxiety and depression. Another section of the reports mentions chronic post-traumatic stress disorder.

However, it should be noted that the psychosocial reports are based on what the female claimant told the case workers. While the female claimant may have these symptoms, the panel is tasked with independently assessing the female claimant's credibility. The panel can accept that the claimants lost a child in 1995 and that they were stopped and threatened by individuals on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2009. However, for the reasons that have already been explained, the panel does not believe that the male claimant filed a complaint against these individuals and does not believe the threats that allegedly ensued. Also, the panel concluded that there is no prospective risk on a balance of probabilities.

It should be noted that despite the fact that the female claimant has been in Canada since XXXX 2009, she allegedly still has post-traumatic disorder according to the reports dated 2011 and early 2012. In addition, the reports do not indicate that her health condition would be compromised if the female claimant had to return to Mexico, as alleged by the claimants and their counsel.

In conclusion, the panel is not of the opinion that the female claimant's psychological health would warrant allowing her claim for refugee protection: the panel does not believe that she would face a serious possibility of persecution, or that she would likely face a risk to her life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if she were to return to her country.

The panel determines that the claimants failed to establish a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that, on a balance of probabilities, they would be personally subjected to a danger of torture, to a risk to their lives or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if they were to return to their country.

Consequently, their claims for refugee protection (and the claim of their minor son) are rejected.
